findings.finding: Insights: Final scores are 20‑bit win patterns; pairing only within equal scores lets any “stable‑matching” of faster vs slower in each group. Ordering count N = product over all groups of (size)! (permutations of tied scores). Compute v₂(N), v₅(N) via Σ vₚ(group!); groups sizes are powers of 2 from 2^{20} down to 1. Use Legendre: vₚ(2^m!) = (2^m−sₚ(2^m))/(p−1). Sum for p=2,5. k = min(v₂(N),v₅(N)) mod 10⁵.

Insights: Scores = 20‑bit win vectors; pairing forces equal‑score groups; faster always gets 1, slower 0 each round. Thus final binary strings are exactly the “binary tournament tree” orderings, i.e. all permutations consistent with the total speed order. Compute N = number of linear extensions of this binary tree (Catalan‑related). Find highest power of 10 dividing N, then k mod 10⁵.

Insights: After 20 rounds each runner’s score is a unique 20‑bit binary number (0…2²⁰‑1). Rankings equal the permutation mapping speed order (1…2²⁰) to these binary numbers. Count N = #bijections realizable by pairing equal‑score players each round. Compute v₂(N), v₅(N); k = min(v₂,v₅). Avoid assuming all 2²⁰! permutations possible—pairing constraints limit N. Use recursive counting of possible assignments per round. Ensure correct handling of factorial factors and powers of 2/5.

Insights: After i rounds each binary win‑string of length i appears on exactly 2^{20‑i} runners, so after 20 rounds every runner has a unique 20‑bit score. Pairings only decide which runner gets which binary string.  
Result: N = (2^{20})! (all permutations possible).  
Thus v₂(N)=∑_{j≥1}⌊2^{20}/2^{j}⌋, v₅(N)=∑_{j≥1}⌊2^{20}/5^{j}⌋.  
k = min(v₂,v₅); compute k mod 10⁵.  
Pitfall: assuming ties; actually scores are distinct, giving full factorial.

Insights: Final scores are binary strings of 20 bits; winner of a round gets a 1 in that bit, loser 0. Within each round, players with identical higher‑bit prefix are paired arbitrarily; faster always wins. Thus any total order of players consistent with the partial order “if A beats B then A’s binary string > B’s” can occur. This poset is exactly the Boolean lattice of 20 bits ordered by componentwise ≤, with each element realized by a unique player. Hence N equals the number of linear extensions of the 20‑dimensional Boolean lattice, i.e. the number of topological sorts of the hypercube DAG. Known formula: N = ∏_{i=0}^{2^{20}-1} (i+1)^{\binom{20}{\operatorname{popcount}(i)}} / (2^{20})! . Compute v₂(N) and v₅(N) via Legendre’s formula on factorials and the product; k = min(v₂,v₅). Finally output k mod 10⁵.

Insights: Final scores are 20‑bit strings; each round halves each equal‑score group, winners get a 1‑bit. Within a group any subset of size half can be winners iff a perfect matching exists pairing each winner with a slower loser (Hall’s condition). Count all possible total orders from such matchings, then compute v₂(N), v₅(N) and k=min(v₂,v₅) mod 10⁵. Pitfalls: assuming winners are always fastest half; must enforce Hall’s condition. Use combinatorial enumeration of feasible winner sets per round.

Insights: After each round every score‑group splits evenly (half win, half lose), so after 20 rounds each of the 2²⁰ binary win‑patterns appears exactly once → final scores are all distinct. Thus rankings are permutations of the runners. N = #permutations realizable by some valid pairing schedule. The process is a binary tournament tree: at round i each current group of size 2^{20‑i+1} is paired arbitrarily, half win (move to “1” branch) half lose (move to “0” branch). Hence any binary tree where each internal node’s two children are unordered (pairings can be any perfect matching) is possible. Counting distinct leaf orderings equals product over all internal nodes of (size/2)! (choices of which players win). So N = ∏_{i=1}^{20} (2^{20‑i})!^{2^{i‑1}}. Compute v₅(N)=∑_{i=1}^{20} 2^{i‑1}·v₅((2^{20‑i})!). Use Legendre: v₅(m!)= (m‑s₅(m))/4 where s₅ sum of base‑5 digits. Sum gives v₅(N)=… then k=v₅(N) (2‑exponent larger). Finally output k mod 10⁵. (Key pitfall: ensure no ties; use correct exponent formula.)

Insights: Final scores are distinct binary strings (0‑2²⁰‑1). Pairings only decide which runner gets which string, respecting that in each match the faster runner must receive the “1” (win) and slower the “0”. Thus the set of possible rankings equals the number of linear extensions of the poset where each runner is constrained to be larger than any slower runner it ever beats (i.e., the “binary heap” order). This poset is the product of chains of lengths 1,2,…,2²⁰‑1, whose extension count N = ∏_{i=1}^{2²⁰‑1} C(i,⌊i/2⌋). Compute v₅(N)=∑_{i} v₅(C(i,⌊i/2⌋)). Use Legendre’s formula for each binomial; sum over i up to 2²⁰‑1. v₂(N) is larger, so k=v₅(N). Finally output k mod 10⁵. Pitfall: ensure correct handling of floor(i/2) and large sums (use Python big‑int).

Insights: Scores are 20‑bit strings, all distinct. A round’s winners must be a “ballot” subset of size half, counted by Catalan C_{2^{j}} for a group of size 2^{j+1}.  
Thus N = ∏_{j=1}^{19} C_{2^{j}}^{2^{19‑j}}.  
Compute v₅(C_{2^{j}}) via Legendre: v₅(C_n)=v₅((2n)!)-2v₅(n!)-v₅(n+1).  
Sum e_j·v₅(C_{2^{j}}) with e_j=2^{19‑j} → v₅(N)=121 818.  
v₂(N)=524 287>v₅, so k=v₅(N)=121 818.  
Answer: k mod 10⁵ = 21 818.  

Pitfalls: assuming any half can win (false); need ballot condition → Catalan count. Use exact vₚ formulas; avoid overflow by summing exponents, not computing N.

Insights: Winners (bit 1) must be paired with slower losers → in speed order, any prefix has ≥ as many losers as winners (ballot/Dyck condition). Recursively apply at each round: each node’s 2^{k‑1} winners/losers must satisfy the same condition within its subset. Thus a final ranking corresponds to labeling the 2^{20} binary strings (leaves of a full binary tree) with the runners so that for every internal node, the set of “1‑leaves” is a Dyck‑compatible subset of its leaves. Counting such labelings gives N. Pitfalls: assuming winners must be top half (false); need recursive Dyck constraints, not just global. Use the product formula N = ∏_{node} C(size(node)/2) where C(n)= (2n)!/(n!·(n+1)!) (Catalan) or equivalent factorial ratios; then compute v₂(N), v₅(N) and k = min(v₂,v₅). Compute k mod 10⁵.

Insights: Each round splits a group of 2m players into m winners + m losers. Feasible splits ⇔ “winner/loser” word is a Dyck word ⇒ Cₘ ways (Catalan). Recursively, every node of size 2^{k} contributes C_{2^{k-1}}.  

Tree: depth 20, level i (0‑based) has 2^{i} nodes of size 2^{20‑i}.  

Total orderings  
\(N=\prod_{i=0}^{19}\big(C_{2^{19-i}}\big)^{2^{i}}\) with \(C_m=\frac1{m+1}\binom{2m}{m}\).  

Compute exponent of 10 in N: find ν₁₀(N)=min(ν₂(N),ν₅(N)). Use Legendre’s formula on each factor; sum over levels.  

Pitfall: ensure Catalan count (Dyck) not “≤” condition; fastest can be winner. Use Cₘ, not binomial alone.  

Result: k=ν₁₀(N); answer = k mod 10⁵.

Insights: After each round, groups of equal score split into winners/losers. In a group of size 2m, any set of m winners is feasible iff the win/lose sequence (fast→slow) is a Dyck word → Catalan Cₘ choices.  

Round r (1‑20): groups = 2^{r‑1}, size = 2^{21‑r}, winners = 2^{20‑r}.  

Thus total assignments (bijections of participants to 20‑bit scores)  

\(N=\prod_{r=1}^{20}\big(C_{2^{20-r}}\big)^{2^{r-1}}
=\prod_{j=0}^{19}\big(C_{2^{j}}\big)^{2^{19-j}}\).

Compute v₂(N), v₅(N) from Catalan formula \(C_n=\frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}\).  
Use Legendre: v_p(C_n)=v_p((2n)!)-2v_p(n!)-v_p(n+1).  
Sum over j with multiplicities 2^{19‑j}.  
k = min(v₂(N),v₅(N)). Return k mod 10⁵.

Insights: Winners/losers split each 2m‑group via a non‑crossing perfect matching → winner set ⇔ Catalan Cₘ possibilities. Recursively, tournament builds a full binary tree whose leaves are runners in speed order; each internal node’s left/right children are winner/loser subsets obeying Catalan rule. Thus any final ranking corresponds to a leaf‑labelled binary tree (inorder = speed order). Count distinct leaf‑orderings = number of distinct binary‑tree labelings = product of Catalan numbers for all internal node sizes? (Key step: show each ranking uniquely determines the tree, so N = ∏_{k=1}^{2^{20}-1} C_{size(k)/2}). Compute v₂(N), v₅(N) via Legendre sums; k = min(v₂,v₅). Return k mod 10⁵. Pitfalls: ensure each ranking ↔ unique tree; avoid overcounting pairings that give same ranking. Use Catalan Cₘ = (2m choose m)/(m+1). Compute exponents efficiently.
